name: Vitamin C
short: Cohort data link supplemental vitamin C to a higher risk of kidney stones in men but not in women. A review advises caution with high doses in susceptible people.
text: In a prospective cohort analysis of 156,735 women and 40,536 men, total and supplemental vitamin C intake was associated with a higher risk of kidney stones in men (hazard ratio 1.19 in the highest supplement category) but not in women, and vitamin C from food was not associated with stones. A meta-analysis of four studies likewise found ascorbic acid supplements associated with a higher incidence of kidney stones in men but not in women; these are observational associations and do not prove cause. A review described vitamin C as relatively safe but advised caution with high doses, which can cause side effects such as oxalate kidney stones in some susceptible patients. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
